_comment: Everything the container needs in order to offer, fetch and install a package.
The dashboard's Tools tab renders it and `bb sdk` acts on it; adding a package
here is the whole job, as long as it fits one of the five kinds below.
name     what `bb sdk install|remove` is called with.
probe    where it lands, so the page can tell installed from not: a bare
name is a directory under the SDK root, android:<pkg> a package
directory under ANDROID_HOME. System images are not packages;
they have a section of their own, above.
platforms  which <os>/<arch> this recipe actually works on. Seven of these
name linux-x86_64 in their URL, and swift names ubuntu24.04, so
"Linux" is not one platform here. `*` in the arch position means
the payload is arch-independent — shell and jars, a git clone, or
a tool that resolves its own platform. An install onto a node
outside the list is refused by name rather than downloading a
couple of hundred megabytes and failing on exec.
requires   other packages this one needs in order to work. Installed
first, and only when missing. android-tools drives sdkmanager,
which is a Java program, and without this it failed inside
sdkmanager with a message naming neither Java nor the package
that supplies it.
layout     where this package lands, once, for everybody who needs to
know. `bin` are directories under it to put on PATH, `env` the
variables it sets (valued as a path under it, "" meaning the
package directory itself), `tool` the file whose presence
proves it is installed, and `reports` the name the census
summary calls it. Written here because it was written in four
places — sdk_env_snippet, the agent's STORE_TOOLS and
STORE_PATHS, and sdk_check_one — and they drifted three times
in one day.
A path may start `root:` to mean relative to the store rather
than to this package — the android packages share one tree,
since sdkmanager installs into <root>/android whatever the
package is called.
system   the machine's own packages this one needs at runtime, by
package manager: `apt` for the Debian family. A recipe runs
as the job account, so the AGENT installs these first, as
root, on a node it may administer (a managed one); on any
other it names them and carries on, and the tool says which
are missing when it is used. Playwright's browsers are the
case: forty libraries the image gets from install-deps and a
node got from nowhere.
source   how to get it. {dir} is the install directory, {version} whatever
the version resolver returned, {script} a downloaded installer.
kind: tarball      resolve a version, fetch source.url, unpack with strip.
script       fetch source.url and run it with the given args and env.
git          shallow-clone a branch; the tool then updates in place.
command      run something already in the image, pointed at {dir}.
sdkmanager   an android package, installed by sdkmanager.
fresh_only   refuse when the directory already exists, for the recipes that
unpack rather than merge.
verify       run after installing, so a broken unpack fails the install
rather than waiting to fail the first time somebody uses it.
time upstream ships: what a package weighs is measured from the disk once it
is installed, remembered after it is removed, and read from the download's
own Content-Length before that when the URL is the payload itself.
download   how to find out what an install would fetch, for a row that is
not installed yet. Absent means source.url is the payload and
its Content-Length is the answer; "command-urls" runs a dry run
and matches the URLs out of it, which is how playwright's five
bundles and the .NET archive are counted. A recipe that cannot
and the row shows no size until it has been installed once.
No size is written down here. One typed into a file is wrong the next time
upstream ships: a row shows what the package takes on this disk once it is
installed, what it took the last time it was, or what the download weighs
before that — never a number somebody guessed.
"url-matches" fetches a file upstream publishes and matches the
URLs out of it, which is how rust's three minimal-profile
components are counted; "android-repo" reads sdkmanager's own
index, keyed by the package id an install resolves to; and
"approximate" is a number written down, for the one recipe whose
download cannot be measured before it happens — a git clone has
no content length. It is marked as an approximation everywhere
it is shown.
System images, which are not packages. A package is one thing at one
version; a system image exists at every API level at once, and which of
them you want is a question about what you are testing, not about the
catalog. So the flavors live here as data, and the Tools tab offers an
API level and a flavor rather than a row per flavor that could only
ever install the newest one.
abi      the only one an x86_64 host can run at any speed.
xml      sdkmanager's own index for that flavor: what levels exist,
and what each weighs before it is downloaded.
about    which one to pick, which is the whole question.

google_apis.label: Google APIs
google_apis.about: Google Play services — Maps, sign-in, push — but no Play Store app. Rootable: `adb root` works, which the Play Store images refuse. This is the default, and what bb emu create fetches.

google_apis_playstore.label: Google APIs + Play Store
google_apis_playstore.about: The same, plus the Play Store app itself — for anything that has to sign in to Play, check a license or take an in-app payment. A Play-certified build, so it is not rootable. Google ships it as a separate image; there is no image that is one plus a switch.

android-wear.label: Wear OS
android-wear.about: What modern Galaxy and Pixel watches run. Round screen, tiny API level numbers of its own.

packages.name: jdk
packages.label: JDK 21 (Temurin)
packages.about: A Java runtime for sdkmanager, Gradle and the emulator tooling. The image carries one; a node's packages store does not, so this is the first thing a node needs for Android work.

packages.name: android-tools
packages.label: Android command-line tools
packages.about: sdkmanager and avdmanager — the bootstrap every other android:* package installs through. The image carries it under /opt/android-sdk; a node installs it here, and its ANDROID_HOME is the store's android/ directory.

run: { command -v unzip >/dev/null 2>&1 && unzip -q "$1" -d "$2"; } || python3 -c "import os,sys,zipfile;z=zipfile.ZipFile(sys.argv[1]);[(z.extract(i,sys.argv[2]), (i.external_attr>>16) and os.chmod(os.path.join(sys.argv[2],i.filename), i.external_attr>>16)) for i in z.infolist()]" "$1" "$2" && root="$(dirname "$2")/android" && mkdir -p "$root/cmdline-tools" && rm -rf "$root/cmdline-tools/latest" && ln -sfn "$2/cmdline-tools" "$root/cmdline-tools/latest"
after: system images and the emulator install through it: bb sdk install android:emulator, bb sdk images

packages.name: android:cmake
packages.label: Android CMake
packages.about: The CMake the NDK's build system uses.

packages.name: android:emulator
packages.label: Android emulator
packages.about: The emulator binary. System images are per API level and come from the image picker above, or from bb emu create on the node.

packages.name: android:platform-tools
packages.label: Android platform tools
packages.about: adb, and the rest of the tools that talk to a device or an emulator. Every `bb emu` verb goes through adb, so the emulator is unusable without it.

packages.name: android:ndk
packages.label: Android NDK
packages.about: Native development kit, for C and C++ inside an Android app.

packages.name: flutter
packages.label: Flutter
packages.about: Flutter with the bundled Dart SDK. Builds Android APKs here; the iOS half of a Flutter app still needs a Mac.

source.warm_note: warming the toolchain (downloads the bundled dart sdk)

packages.name: go
packages.label: Go
packages.about: Cross-compiles from here to Windows, macOS, Linux and ARM with GOOS and GOARCH — no extra toolchain, no target to install.

packages.name: dotnet
packages.label: .NET + MAUI
packages.about: The .NET SDK plus the maui-android workload — Android apps from C#.

then.note: adding the maui-android workload (android targets from C#)
then.optional: the maui-android workload failed; the plain SDK is still installed

packages.name: node
packages.label: Node.js
packages.about: The JavaScript runtime and npm. Not needed to BE a node — the agent is Python and the provisioner installs that — but a project built with npm needs it here, and so does anything that drives a browser through Playwright.

packages.name: playwright
packages.label: Playwright browsers
packages.about: Chromium, Firefox and WebKit, and the playwright module that drives them, together in the store. The image carries a copy of the module and the system libraries; a node carries neither, so the module lands here beside the browsers and NODE_PATH points at it — what bb shot and the dashboard's own tests require().

run: npm install --prefix "$1" --no-audit --no-fund --loglevel=error playwright@latest && "$1/node_modules/.bin/playwright" install chromium firefox webkit

packages.name: lint-tools
packages.label: Lint tools (shellcheck, hadolint, actionlint, ruff, yq, fd)
packages.about: What bb lint runs: shellcheck, hadolint, actionlint and ruff, with yq and fd beside them. The image carries all six; a node's store does not, so bb lint on a node skips its checks until this is installed. Static binaries from each project's latest GitHub release.

run: dst="$2/bin"; t="$(mktemp -d)"; mkdir -p "$dst"; cp "$1" "$dst/hadolint"; get() { curl -fsSL --retry 3 -o "$2" "$1"; }; tag() { curl -fsSIL -o /dev/null -w '%{url_effective}' "https://github.com/$1/releases/latest" | sed 's#.*/tag/##'; }; get https://github.com/mikefarah/yq/releases/latest/download/yq_linux_amd64 "$dst/yq"; get https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/releases/latest/download/ruff-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz "$t/ruff.tgz"; tar -xzf "$t/ruff.tgz" -C "$t"; cp "$(find "$t" -name ruff -type f | head -1)" "$dst/"; v="$(tag koalaman/shellcheck)"; get "https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck/releases/download/$v/shellcheck-$v.linux.x86_64.tar.xz" "$t/sc.txz"; tar -xJf "$t/sc.txz" -C "$t"; cp "$t/shellcheck-$v/shellcheck" "$dst/"; v="$(tag rhysd/actionlint)"; get "https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint/releases/download/$v/actionlint_${v#v}_linux_amd64.tar.gz" "$t/al.tgz"; tar -xzf "$t/al.tgz" -C "$t" actionlint; cp "$t/actionlint" "$dst/"; v="$(tag sharkdp/fd)"; get "https://github.com/sharkdp/fd/releases/download/$v/fd-$v-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz" "$t/fd.tgz"; tar -xzf "$t/fd.tgz" -C "$t"; cp "$(find "$t" -name fd -type f | head -1)" "$dst/"; chmod +x "$dst"/*; rm -rf "$t"

packages.name: rust
packages.label: Rust
packages.about: rustup, cargo and the stable toolchain, kept in one directory. A Windows target needs a linker as well: gcc-mingw-w64 via EXTRA_APT_PACKAGES, or zig plus cargo-zigbuild.

after: a Windows target also needs a linker: rustup target add x86_64-pc-windows-gnu,
then EXTRA_APT_PACKAGES=gcc-mingw-w64, or bb sdk install zig + cargo-zigbuild

packages.name: swift
packages.label: Swift
packages.about: The Swift toolchain for Linux: shared logic, server-side Swift, and compiling packages. Not an iOS SDK.

packages.name: zig
packages.label: Zig
packages.about: A C and C++ cross-compiler as much as a language: `zig cc -target x86_64-windows-gnu` turns this box into a Windows toolchain, and it links for Rust too.
